A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MagicDec, with matching core analysis and identifiable shared experiments. Text, equations, figures, and tables are readable throughout. v1 ends with references; v4 includes a fully available Appendix A.1–A.6.

before.justification: v1 Section 5, Figure 5, and Tables 1–2 report original PG-19 experiments measuring decoding latency and speedup on A100, L40, and H100 GPUs.

after.justification: v4 Sections 4–5 and Appendix A report original acceptance-rate and speedup measurements on PG-19 and RULER tasks, including additional model and inference-backend comparisons.

M1.justification: v1 Section 4 uses StreamingLLM caches for self-speculation and standalone drafts. v4 Section 4 expands drafting into a framework for selecting the compression algorithm, KV budget, and draft model using acceptance rate and decoding/search costs, and adds SnapKV-based self-speculation. This changes draft-cache construction while retaining the underlying speculative verification framework.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates book-text generation on PG-19. v4 retains PG-19 and adds RULER needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, common-word extraction, and QA-1 tasks (Figure 5 and Table 2), substantially extending the task requirements represented in evaluation.

E2.justification: v4 adds evaluated comparisons involving SnapKV, PQCache, top-k attention, and full-cache versus StreamingLLM-cache LLaMA-3.2-1B drafts (Figures 4, 5, and 7). TinyLLaMA comparisons remain in the appendices, but its comparator rows are removed from the corresponding L40/H100 comparison in v4 Table 1.

E3.justification: The stated PG-19 protocol changes from 50 samples generating 64 tokens in v1 Section 5.1 to 20 batches generating 96 tokens in v4 Section 5.1. v4 also adds Qwen/Mistral model configurations and 8-H100 evaluations. Retained H100 rows are labeled with KV budget 512 rather than v1's 256; their unchanged timings do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's budget, speculation-length, and batch/context sweeps, v4 adds acceptance-versus-selection-cost analyses, minimum acceptance requirements for 1.8x speedup, and task-dependent static/dynamic KV-selection comparisons (Figures 4c and 5). Figure 7 examines draft-model tradeoffs, while Appendix A.3 tests dependence on the inference backend.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the experimental results. The change from 50 samples to 20 batches concerns evaluation sample size, not repeated-run or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Much of v1 Table 1 survives in v4 Table 3, but substantial new results appear. These include 2.51x SnapKV self-speculation speedup on CWE with 100,000-token context, batch size 41, and 8 H100 GPUs (Table 2), plus Qwen/Mistral and backend results. These are additional experimental settings, not same-setting improvements over v1's A100 headline results.

T1.justification: The expected-token formula and critical-sequence-length analysis already exist in v1. v4 Section 4.1 substantially extends the mathematical model by defining KV-selection cost and total compressed-cache drafting cost, then introducing an optimization objective over selection strategy, budget, speculation length, and acceptance rate (Equations 3–4).

C1.justification: The claim that speculative decoding can improve both latency and throughput without quality loss is retained. v4 adds a general drafting-strategy selection framework as a central contribution and claims that KV compression achieves higher acceptance than model compression under comparable memory constraints. This broadens v1's contribution centered on large-batch viability with StreamingLLM drafting.

C2.justification: v4 explains task-dependent static-versus-dynamic selection tradeoffs and why top-k selection can be impractical despite high acceptance (Section 4.4). Section 6 explicitly limits the work to decoding rather than prefill and discusses deployment constraints on commodity hardware. These substantive interpretations and applicability qualifications go beyond v1's bottleneck and budget discussion.

D1.justification: v1 documents FlashAttention-2 and custom GQA pseudocode. v4 Appendix A.1 instead documents Flashinfer, MLC-LLM, torch.compile, Triton MLP operations, and embedding-layer tensor parallelism. It also supplies SnapKV and PQCache parameters and explains backend timing conventions. Conversely, v1's direct MagicDec code link and custom GQA pseudocode are absent from v4.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning around KV-compression research, including SnapKV, PQCache, Quest, and other selection methods, and discusses complementarity with Speculation Parallelism. The retained TriForce connection is reframed around choosing among compression strategies rather than primarily motivating StreamingLLM drafting; v1's BASS discussion is removed.

P1.justification: The introduction and theoretical narrative are extensively rewritten around three insights and a drafting-selection framework. Method and evaluation sections are reorganized, implementation and supporting results move into a new appendix, and the conclusion gains explicit limitations. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v4 replaces and redraws introductory and analytical displays, adds acceptance/tradeoff plots and a system diagram, and expands the result-table layouts. v1 Figure 5 is split across v4 Figures 6 and 9, while its main A100 table moves to Appendix Table 3. Conference formatting also changes the document's typography and page layout.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the basis for choosing drafting strategies: Section 4 explicitly models selection overhead, task-dependent comparisons test the resulting tradeoffs, and Appendix A examines backend and model dependence. This addresses v1's limited StreamingLLM/PG-19 support for broader recommendations, while explicit decoding-only limitations clarify scope. These gains outweigh the loss of the direct code link and ambiguity introduced by relabeling retained H100 results.
